name: Argentina
system: Federal presidential republic with a bicameral National Congress

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: No majority; La Libertad Avanza is the largest bloc and relies on allied and provincial blocs to pass legislation
legislature.detail: 257 seats. In the October 2025 midterm, La Libertad Avanza won about 40.8% and 64 of the 127 seats contested, and Fuerza Patria won about 24.5% and 31 seats. When the new chamber was sworn in in December 2025, La Libertad Avanza had 95 seats and Unión por la Patria 93.

legislature.name: Senate
legislature.control: No majority; the Peronist interbloc remains the largest group, but in February 2026 a La Libertad Avanza-led alliance with the UCR, PRO and provincial senators won 45 votes to fill the chamber's leadership posts, leaving the Peronist interbloc without any
legislature.detail: 72 seats. Since February 2026: Peronist interbloc 25, La Libertad Avanza 21, UCR 10, the Impulso País interbloc (PRO, Provincias Unidas and provincial senators) 7, and Convicción Federal 3, formed by senators who left the Peronist interbloc; the rest sit in provincial blocs.

judiciary: The Supreme Court of Justice is the highest court. Only three of its five seats are filled, by Horacio Rosatti, Carlos Rosenkrantz and Ricardo Lorenzetti. In 2026 President Milei put off nominating anyone to the two vacancies, and many lower federal judgeships are also vacant.

elections.name: Legislative midterm election (half of the Chamber of Deputies, one-third of the Senate)
elections.note: La Libertad Avanza won about 40.8% of the national vote for the Chamber of Deputies and 64 seats, ahead of the Peronist Fuerza Patria at about 24.5% and 31 seats. This made it the largest bloc in the Chamber of Deputies and increased its seats in the Senate.

elections.name: General election (president, vice-president and partial renewal of Congress)
elections.note: Under current law the election falls on the fourth Sunday of October, with a runoff in November if needed. The government is seeking to suspend the PASO primaries.

synopsis: Libertarian economist Javier Milei of La Libertad Avanza has been president since December 2023. He has pursued deep spending cuts, deregulation and disinflation. His party became the largest bloc in the Chamber of Deputies after winning the October 2025 midterms but still needs allies to pass laws, and Diego Santilli has been Chief of the Cabinet of Ministers since June 2026.
policies: Fiscal austerity and a balanced-budget target, set out in the 2027 budget bill now before Congress
Disinflation and reform of the Central Bank
Labour market reform (Labour Modernisation Law passed in February 2026)
Deregulation and incentives for large investments, including data centres and AI
Changes to electoral rules, including suspending the PASO primaries
challenges: Inflation remains persistent: 2.2% month-on-month and 33.1% year-on-year in October 2026
Building legislative majorities with governors and allied blocs for the 2027 budget
Social pressure over spending cuts to universities, disability programmes and transport subsidies
Vacancies on the Supreme Court and throughout the federal judiciary
Corruption investigations touching officials, including the inquiry that preceded Chief of Cabinet Manuel Adorni's resignation in June 2026

name: Bolivia
system: Presidential republic (Plurinational State) with a bicameral Plurinational Legislative Assembly

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: No majority; the PDC is the largest group. The Unidad alliance ended its relationship with the government in July 2026 and calls itself a constructive opposition
legislature.detail: 130 seats (2025 election): PDC 49, Libre 39, Unidad 26, Alianza Popular 8, APB Súmate 5, MAS-IPSP 2, BIA-YUQUI 1; 66 needed for a majority. President: Roberto Castro (PDC)

legislature.name: Chamber of Senators
legislature.control: No majority; the PDC is the largest group
legislature.detail: 36 seats (2025 election): PDC 16, Libre 12, Unidad 7, APB Súmate 1. President: Diego Ávila (PDC), re-elected for the 2026-2027 session

judiciary: The highest courts are the Supreme Court of Justice and the Plurinational Constitutional Tribunal, whose judges are chosen by popular vote; the partial 2024 judicial elections left seats empty that have still not been filled. In its first year the Paz government also faced challenges over judicial matters.

elections.name: General election (president, vice president and Plurinational Legislative Assembly), runoff
elections.note: First round held on 17 August 2025, when no party won a majority in either chamber. In the runoff, Rodrigo Paz (PDC) beat former president Jorge 'Tuto' Quiroga (Libre) with about 55% of the vote to 45%, ending nearly two decades of MAS governments.

elections.name: Subnational elections (governors, mayors, councils and departmental assemblies)
elections.note: Governor runoffs followed on 19 April 2026. Candidates backed by the government won two of the nine governorships, La Paz and Beni; in La Paz, Luis Revilla led the first round with about 20% and was declared governor after his runoff opponent withdrew. The MAS kept Cochabamba, and an opposition candidate won Tarija, President Paz's home region.

elections.name: General election
elections.note: Due by law at the end of the five-year term

synopsis: Rodrigo Paz of the centrist Christian Democratic Party took office on 8 November 2025 after winning Bolivia's first presidential runoff, ending nearly two decades of MAS rule. His government does not have a majority in the legislature. It came through weeks of road blockades and protests, including calls for the president's resignation, in May and June 2026, and has had a long public falling-out with Vice President Edmand Lara.
policies: Measures to stabilise the economy and address shortages of fuel and foreign currency
Austerity and fiscal adjustment measures
Moving the economy away from the state-led model of the MAS years
A nationwide state of emergency in June 2026 that let the armed forces clear road blockades
challenges: Economic crisis, with high living costs and an unfinished economic stabilisation
Social unrest: about 50 days of blockades and calls for the president to resign in May and June 2026
Open conflict between President Paz and Vice President Lara, who presides over the legislature
No legislative majority after the Unidad alliance broke with the government in July 2026
Empty seats on the top courts and delays to new judicial elections
reviewNote: The official runoff percentage could not be confirmed: sources give between 54.4% and 54.96% for Paz, so the record says about 55%. Roberto Castro as president of the Chamber of Deputies for 2026-2027 rests on one report (Opinión) of the opening of the session on 11 November 2026, which does not give his party. AP described Paz in April 2026 as having no party of his own; the record keeps the PDC, on whose ticket he was elected, as his party and the governing party, which needs checking. The date of any judicial election in late 2026 was not confirmed.

name: Brazil

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: No single-party majority; centre-right and right-wing parties hold most seats. The largest party is the opposition Liberal Party (PL). The chamber is presided over by Hugo Motta (Republicanos).
legislature.detail: The 4 October 2026 election filled all 513 seats for the term starting 1 February 2027. Results: Liberal Party (PL) 121; Brazil of Hope federation (PT-PCdoB-PV) 88 (70 of them PT); Progressive Union federation (União Brasil-PP) 87; PSD 43; Republicanos 41; MDB 36; Podemos 27; others 70.

legislature.name: Federal Senate
legislature.control: No single-party majority; centre-right and right-wing parties hold most seats. The largest bloc is the opposition Liberal Party (PL). The Senate is presided over by Davi Alcolumbre (União Brasil).
legislature.detail: The 4 October 2026 election filled 54 of the 81 seats, and the PL won 19 of them. From February 2027 the PL is reported to hold 28 or 29 seats (sources differ), against 9 for the PT and 8 for the MDB.

judiciary: The Supreme Federal Court (STF), led by Chief Justice Edson Fachin, is the highest constitutional court. The Superior Electoral Court (TSE), presided over by Kassio Nunes Marques, runs elections. In 2026 the STF went through an internal crisis: justices clashed with each other over the Banco Master fraud scandal. A last-minute ruling by Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting hours in the October 2026 runoff became the basis of Flávio Bolsonaro's call to annul the result.

elections.name: General election (first round: president, Congress, governors)
elections.note: Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) led the presidential vote with 47.03% to Lula's 45.16%. The PL won 121 Chamber seats and 19 of the 54 Senate seats contested.

elections.name: Presidential runoff
elections.note: Lula (PT) won a fourth, non-consecutive term with about 51.8% of valid votes to Flávio Bolsonaro's 48.2%. It is the first time a first-round runner-up has won a Brazilian presidential election. Bolsonaro refused to concede and said he would seek annulment; the next day he dropped that plan in favour of electoral-court actions seeking to remove Lula's ticket, and the PL accepted the TSE-certified result. The inauguration is scheduled for 5 January 2027.

synopsis: Lula da Silva of the Workers' Party won a fourth, non-consecutive term in the 25 October 2026 runoff, coming back after losing the first round to Flávio Bolsonaro, and is due to be sworn in for the new term on 5 January 2027. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party became the largest party in both houses of the Congress elected in October 2026, so Lula will need support from centrist parties. He is negotiating cabinet posts with the PSD, MDB, União Brasil, PP and Republicanos.
policies: Fiscal plan seeking to address slow growth and high interest rates, relying mainly on revenue measures such as curbing tax breaks and raising levies on higher-income groups
Coalition-building with centrist parties through cabinet appointments ahead of the 2027 term
Cutting Amazon deforestation and climate diplomacy, including attending COP31, while also backing large oil exploration projects
Expanding Brazil's international role, including through BRICS
challenges: A Congress with a stronger right wing, where the opposition PL is the largest party in both chambers
Fiscal pressures from fast-growing mandatory spending, high debt-servicing costs and a weak real
Political polarisation, including Flávio Bolsonaro's refusal to accept the runoff result and his departure for the United States
An internal crisis at the Supreme Federal Court linked to the Banco Master fraud scandal
Strained relations with the United States after the 2025–2026 diplomatic dispute
reviewNote: Not confirmed: which centrist parties (MDB, PSD, União Brasil, PP, Republicanos) still hold ministries in the current cabinet. governingParties lists only the PT and the left-wing parties sources describe as government members. The PL's Senate total from February 2027 is reported as 28 in some sources and 29 in others. The outcome of the electoral-court actions Flávio Bolsonaro's campaign filed against Lula's ticket was not found.

name: Chile
system: Unitary presidential republic with a bicameral National Congress

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: No single bloc has a majority. The left-wing Unidad por Chile is the largest bloc, and the right-wing blocs Cambio por Chile and Chile Grande y Unido together hold about half the seats.
legislature.detail: 155 seats (November 2025): Unidad por Chile 61, Cambio por Chile 42, Chile Grande y Unido 34, Party of the People 14, Greens, Regionalists and Humanists 3, independent 1. Largest party: Republican Party with 31.

legislature.name: Senate
legislature.control: Evenly split. The right-wing blocs hold 25 of the 50 seats; Unidad por Chile and allied or independent senators hold the other 25.
legislature.detail: 50 seats (after the November 2025 partial renewal): Chile Grande y Unido 18, Cambio por Chile 7, Unidad por Chile 20, Greens, Regionalists and Humanists 3, independents 2. Senate President: Paulina Núñez (National Renewal), elected March 2026.

judiciary: The Supreme Court heads the ordinary judiciary, and a separate Constitutional Court reviews whether laws are constitutional.

elections.name: Presidential election (runoff)
elections.note: José Antonio Kast (Republican Party) defeated Jeannette Jara (Unidad por Chile) with about 58% of the vote to about 42%. He took office on 11 March 2026 for the 2026-2030 term.

elections.name: General election (presidential first round, Chamber of Deputies and partial Senate)
elections.note: Unidad por Chile won the most Chamber seats (61 of 155), but the right-wing blocs together came close to a majority. The Senate ended up split 25-25 between right and left.

elections.name: General election (presidential, Chamber of Deputies and partial Senate)
elections.note: A possible presidential runoff would follow in December 2029.

synopsis: José Antonio Kast, who founded the right-wing Republican Party and left it on taking office, won the December 2025 runoff and took office on 11 March 2026. He calls his administration an emergency government, and its cabinet is mostly independents, together with ministers from the Republicans and the traditional right. Congress is closely divided: the left-wing Unidad por Chile is the largest bloc in the Chamber of Deputies, and the Senate is split evenly between right and left.
policies: Priority on immigration control and border security
Public security and crime reduction under an 'emergency government' agenda
Corporate tax cuts and lighter regulation to revive growth
A broad cabinet of independents and ministers from several parties, presented as national unity
challenges: A contracting economy in 2026, driven mainly by falling copper mining output
Passing legislation without a clear majority in either chamber
Keeping together a coalition that runs from the far right to the centre-right
Public concern over crime and irregular migration
reviewNote: Not confirmed: (1) which parties are in the cabinet after the May 2026 reshuffle and any later changes, including whether Evópoli is still represented. A Radical Party member was also in the cabinet, but it is unclear whether the party itself is in government. (2) Whether the National Libertarian Party, which is part of Cambio por Chile, is in government. (3) Seat counts are the November 2025 election results and do not reflect later defections. Sources also disagree on whether the right-wing blocs won 76 or 77 Chamber seats.

name: Colombia
system: Unitary presidential republic with a bicameral Congress

legislature.name: Senate
legislature.control: Pro-government coalition majority: the Democratic Centre, Liberal, Conservative, Party of the U, Radical Change and National Salvation Movement declared themselves government parties in September 2026; Historic Pact is the largest single party and leads the opposition
legislature.detail: 103 seats: 102 elected in March 2026 plus the opposition seat of runner-up presidential candidate Iván Cepeda. Historic Pact 26 (25 elected plus Cepeda), Democratic Centre 17, Liberal Party 13, Conservative Party 10; remaining seats split among smaller parties and the two indigenous seats

legislature.name: Chamber of Representatives
legislature.control: Pro-government coalition majority: the main traditional and right-wing parties declared themselves government parties in September 2026; Historic Pact is the largest single party and leads the opposition
legislature.detail: 183 seats (March 2026 election); Historic Pact the largest party, followed by Democratic Centre, Liberal Party and Conservative Party; exact counts differ between sources

judiciary: The Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court of Justice and the Council of State head the judiciary. In November 2026 the Constitutional Court upheld, with limits, the economic emergency President de la Espriella declared after the 10 August 2026 earthquake: it applies only in affected municipalities, and its funds cannot be used to cover the fiscal deficit or problems that predate the earthquake.

elections.name: Congressional election
elections.note: Fragmented result: Historic Pact came first in both chambers (25 of the 102 elected Senate seats) and Democratic Centre second (17 Senate seats).

elections.name: Presidential election, first round
elections.note: Abelardo de la Espriella 43.7%, Iván Cepeda (Historic Pact) 40.9%.

elections.name: Presidential election, runoff
elections.note: Abelardo de la Espriella won with about 49.7% against Iván Cepeda's 48.7%, a margin of about 252,000 votes in the final count, the narrowest in a Colombian presidential runoff.

elections.name: Regional and municipal elections
elections.note: Elections for governors, departmental assemblies, mayors and councils (not national offices).

elections.name: Presidential election
elections.note: Due by law at the end of the 2026-2030 presidential term.

synopsis: Right-wing lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella took office as president on 7 August 2026 after narrowly beating leftist Iván Cepeda in the June runoff, succeeding Gustavo Petro. He governs with a broad coalition of traditional and right-wing parties in a fragmented Congress in which Petro's Historic Pact is the largest single party and leads the opposition.
policies: A hardline security strategy against armed groups and drug trafficking, replacing the previous government's "total peace" talks
The Submission Law, passed in November 2026, which requires illegal armed groups to submit to the ordinary criminal justice system
Fiscal austerity, including an Economic Rescue Bill that cuts spending and raises taxes
A planned overhaul that would eliminate or merge about half of the national executive branch's agencies
Closer alignment with the United States
challenges: Rising violence, including extortion, kidnappings, homicides and attacks on security forces, in conflict regions
Strained public finances and investor concern about the fiscal outlook
Recovery from the August 2026 earthquake and the economic emergency declared afterwards

Keeping a fragmented congressional coalition together; in July 2026 Historic Pact and Democratic Centre senators backed Honorio Henríquez (Democratic Centre), who defeated the president-elect's preferred candidate for Senate president
Deep political polarisation after the narrowest presidential runoff result on record
reviewNote: Seat counts in the Chamber of Representatives differ between sources (for example, Liberal Party 24 or 26 seats; one Cundinamarca seat was still disputed in July 2026), so only the largest parties are named. Smaller parties that also declared for the government in September 2026 (among them ASI, the Democratic Party, Liga de Gobernantes Anticorrupción and Colombia Justa Libres) are not listed, and their seats are not confirmed. De la Espriella ran for president through the Defensores de la Patria signature movement, with the National Salvation Movement as co-endorser.

name: Ecuador
system: Unitary presidential republic with a unicameral National Assembly

legislature.name: National Assembly (Asamblea Nacional)
legislature.control: National Democratic Action (ADN) and allied legislators (working majority); Assembly President Mishel Mancheno (ADN) since 8 June 2026
legislature.detail: 151 seats; February 2025 election: Citizen Revolution–RETO 67, ADN 66, Pachakutik 9, Social Christian Party 4, others 5. ADN and its allies won the Assembly presidency with support from non-aligned members. The pro-government bloc has since grown to about 78 members.

judiciary: The Constitutional Court reviews laws, states of exception and proposed referendums and constitutional amendments, and the National Court of Justice is the highest court for ordinary cases. The Constitutional Court has repeatedly been in tension with the Noboa government: it has suspended or set conditions on security measures and curfews, admitted challenges to urgent economic laws, and accepted only some of the government's proposed constitutional amendments.

elections.name: Presidential runoff election
elections.note: Daniel Noboa (ADN) defeated Luisa González (Citizen Revolution) with about 55.6% of the vote to 44.4% and began a full four-year term in May 2025.

elections.name: General election (first round and National Assembly)
elections.note: Citizen Revolution–RETO won 67 of 151 Assembly seats and ADN 66; Noboa and González went through to the runoff.

elections.name: Referendum and popular consultation
elections.note: Voters rejected all four questions put forward by Noboa, including a Constituent Assembly to write a new constitution (about 61.8% No) and allowing foreign military bases.

elections.name: Local (sectional) elections and Citizen Participation and Social Control Council (CPCCS) election
elections.note: Brought forward from 14 February 2027. Voters elect 23 prefects, 222 mayors, councillors, parish boards and seven CPCCS councillors; the campaign runs from 12 to 26 November 2026.

elections.name: General election (president and National Assembly)
elections.note: Next presidential and legislative election due by law at the end of the 2025–2029 term.

synopsis: Daniel Noboa of National Democratic Action, first elected in a 2023 snap election, won a full term in April 2025 and governs with a working majority in the National Assembly. His government has focused on a militarized response to organized crime, including repeated states of exception, but voters rejected all four of his referendum questions in November 2025, including a call for a new constitution. Nationwide local elections are scheduled for 29 November 2026.
policies: Militarized security policy against organized crime and drug-trafficking gangs, including repeated states of exception, curfews and a larger military role in internal security
Building new maximum-security prisons, such as El Encuentro in Santa Elena, which began receiving prisoners in November 2025
Economic reforms passed through urgent economic bills sent to the National Assembly
Constitutional amendments to take the power to appoint officials away from the Citizen Participation and Social Control Council (CPCCS)
challenges: High levels of violent crime and gang activity, with states of exception renewed across several provinces
Legal disputes with the Constitutional Court over security measures and urgent laws
Voters' rejection of the government's November 2025 referendum proposals, including a new constitution
Human rights concerns raised about the use of the military in internal security
Frequent elections: the November 2026 local vote is the sixth electoral process in less than four years
reviewNote: Not confirmed: the Social Christian Party's February 2025 seat count (4 on its own, 5 with an allied list in some sources), and the current size of the pro-government bloc (about 78 members, from a single source).

name: Guyana
system: Unitary presidential republic with an executive president who is elected through the winning party list, and a unicameral National Assembly

legislature.name: National Assembly
legislature.control: People's Progressive Party/Civic (majority)
legislature.detail: 65 seats after the 1 September 2025 election: PPP/C 36, We Invest in Nationhood (WIN) 16, A Partnership for National Unity (APNU) 12, Forward Guyana Movement (FGM) 1. WIN leader Azruddin Mohamed has been Leader of the Opposition since 26 January 2026.

judiciary: The Court of Appeal and the High Court make up the Supreme Court of Judicature, and the Caribbean Court of Justice is the final court of appeal. Roxane George-Wiltshire (acting Chancellor) and Navindra Singh (acting Chief Justice) have led the judiciary in acting roles since August 2025. In July 2026 the Caribbean Court of Justice dismissed an appeal by Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed and allowed US extradition proceedings against him to continue.

elections.name: General and regional elections
elections.note: PPP/C won 36 of 65 seats and President Irfaan Ali was re-elected; the new WIN party came second with 16 seats, ahead of APNU with 12 and FGM with 1. GECOM declared the result on 6 September 2025, and Ali was sworn in for a second term on 7 September 2025.

elections.name: General and regional elections
elections.note: Due by law; presidential and legislative terms are five years.

synopsis: Guyana is a presidential republic. President Irfaan Ali of the People's Progressive Party/Civic won a second five-year term in September 2025 with a majority in the National Assembly. The new We Invest in Nationhood party replaced APNU as the main opposition. Its leader, Azruddin Mohamed, faces US extradition proceedings and has been held on remand since 30 October 2026 on a separate cybercrime charge. The economy is being reshaped by fast-growing offshore oil production, while the long-running border case with Venezuela over the Essequibo region awaits a final judgment from the International Court of Justice.
policies: Using offshore oil revenue to fund infrastructure, housing and public services
Expanding power generation, including the Wales gas-to-energy project
Seeking a binding ICJ ruling that upholds the 1899 Arbitral Award boundary with Venezuela
Opening housing and infrastructure to foreign investors
Promoting payment for forest conservation in international climate talks
challenges: The territorial claim by Venezuela to the Essequibo region, with the ICJ judgment, which Guyana's government expects between November 2026 and January 2027, still pending
Political tension over the arrest, remand and US extradition proceedings against Opposition Leader Azruddin Mohamed
Deadlock over the make-up of the Guyana Elections Commission, which puts the statutory local government elections at risk
Managing rapid oil-driven growth and electricity supply that falls short of peak demand
Illegal gold mining and security incidents along the borders

name: Peru
system: Unitary presidential republic with a bicameral Congress (restored in 2026)

legislature.name: Senate
legislature.control: No single-party majority; Popular Force is the largest party, and together with Popular Renewal it holds half the seats (30 of 60)
legislature.detail: 60 seats (2026 election): Popular Force 22, Together for Peru 14, Popular Renewal 8, Party of Good Government 7, Works Civic Party 5, Now Nation 4. Speaker: Miki Torres (Popular Force), since 26 July 2026.

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: No majority; Popular Force is the largest party
legislature.detail: 130 seats (2026 election), 66 needed for a majority: Popular Force 41, Together for Peru 32, Party of Good Government 18, Popular Renewal 15, Works Civic Party 14, Now Nation 10. Speaker: Óscar Reto (Party of Good Government), since 26 July 2026.

judiciary: The Constitutional Tribunal, whose members Congress elects, rules on constitutional questions; the Supreme Court of Justice heads the ordinary courts. In recent years Congress has repeatedly clashed with judicial and prosecutorial bodies, and in December 2023 the Tribunal ordered Alberto Fujimori's release despite objections from the Inter-American Court of Human Rights.

elections.name: General election (president first round, Senate and Chamber of Deputies)
elections.note: Keiko Fujimori (Popular Force) won 17.2% and Roberto Sánchez (Together for Peru) 12.0%, so the two went to a runoff. Popular Force became the largest party in both chambers of the restored bicameral Congress.

elections.name: Presidential runoff
elections.note: Keiko Fujimori won with 50.135% of valid votes to 49.865% for Roberto Sánchez, a margin of about 50,000 votes. The National Elections Board (JNE) proclaimed her president-elect on 3 July 2026.

elections.name: General election (president and Congress)
elections.note: Due by law at the end of the five-year term.

synopsis: Keiko Fujimori, leader of the conservative Popular Force, became president on 28 July 2026 after narrowly beating leftist Roberto Sánchez in the runoff. She is Peru's ninth president in a decade. The 2026 election also restored a two-chamber Congress, in which her party is the largest group but has no majority of its own.
policies: A tough approach to crime and extortion, including a larger role for the armed forces in emergency zones
Promoting economic growth and investment, with economist Elmer Cuba as economy minister
Closer security ties with the United States, including joining the US-led Shield of the Americas coalition against transnational crime in September 2026
Measures against crime and for the expected El Niño floods under legislative powers that Congress delegated to the executive in October 2026
challenges: High levels of crime and extortion
Long-running political instability and frequent clashes between the president and Congress
A society split by the very close 2026 runoff
A Congress where the government has no majority of its own
Falling public approval: in October 2026 Ipsos found 49% disapproval and 40% approval, down from 57% approval in August
reviewNote: Not confirmed: whether Luis Galarreta is still President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister) in November 2026; La República reported on 27 October 2026 that the President was considering replacing him. Seat counts are the 2026 election results and do not reflect later changes in parliamentary groups.

name: Paraguay
system: Unitary presidential republic with a bicameral Congress

legislature.name: Chamber of Senators
legislature.control: Colorado Party (ANR) majority, led by the Honor Colorado faction; some Colorado senators sit in separate dissident or independent blocs
legislature.detail: 45 seats, elected in April 2023, when the Colorado Party won 23. On 2026-11-06 all 44 senators present voted to remove President Santiago Peña from office.

legislature.name: Chamber of Deputies
legislature.control: Colorado Party (ANR) majority, led by the Honor Colorado faction
legislature.detail: 80 seats, elected in April 2023. On 2026-11-05 it approved the impeachment charges against Peña by 78 votes.

judiciary: The Supreme Court of Justice is the highest court and also rules on constitutional challenges. The Superior Tribunal of Electoral Justice (TSJE) runs and adjudicates elections. After Santiago Peña was removed, prosecutors charged him over the Ueno Bank collapse and he was placed under house arrest.

elections.name: General election (president, Congress, governors)
elections.note: Santiago Peña of the Colorado Party won the presidency (a single round, decided by plurality), with Pedro Alliana as vice-president. The Colorado Party won majorities in both chambers. Peña was removed by impeachment on 2026-11-06, and Alliana is completing the term, which ends in August 2028.

elections.name: Municipal elections
elections.note: Nationwide local elections. The Colorado Party won a record 187 of 263 mayoralties but lost Asunción to Soledad Núñez (Alianza Juntos por Asunción). It also failed to win Ciudad del Este, where Daniel Pereira Mujica of Yo Creo won.

elections.name: Simultaneous party primaries for the 2028 general election
elections.note: Legally due between 2027-12-12 and 2028-02-13. The TSJE has not yet set the exact date.

elections.name: General election (president, Congress, governors)
elections.note: Due between mid-April and mid-May 2028. The TSJE has not yet set the exact date. The new president takes office in August 2028.

synopsis: Paraguay is a presidential republic long dominated by the conservative Colorado Party, which holds the presidency and majorities in both chambers of Congress. In November 2026, after the collapse of Ueno Bank, President Santiago Peña resigned. Congress impeached and removed him anyway, and Vice-President Pedro Alliana was sworn in on 6 November to finish the term to August 2028. Congress chose Senator Antonio Barrios as the new vice-president.
policies: Alliana has pledged to fully compensate savers affected by the Ueno Bank collapse
Rebuilding the cabinet with a mix of new appointees and members of the previous government, including a new interior minister and a new head of the Civil Cabinet
Promising institutional stability, transparency and a 'pacification' process after Peña's removal
Continuing the market-friendly economic approach of the Colorado governments and close ties with the United States
challenges: Fallout from the Ueno Bank collapse, which accusers in the impeachment trial said cost about 1.2 billion US dollars, and the recovery of savers' deposits
A criminal case against former president Peña over the collapse, with charges of breach of trust and influence peddling
Allegations of conflicts of interest and of mismanaged funds at public bodies, including the social security institute (IPS)
Factional splits within the Colorado Party in Congress, and opposition gains in the largest cities in the 2026 municipal elections
Building political stability before the 2027–28 primary and general election cycle
reviewNote: Not confirmed: the Colorado Party's 2023 seat total in the Chamber of Deputies (sources give 48 or 49 of 80), and developments after about 10 November 2026, including any court challenge to Peña's removal. On 5 November 2026 the Chamber of Deputies rejected impeachment charges against Alliana by 48 votes to 30.

name: Suriname
system: Unitary republic with an executive president elected by the National Assembly; the president is both head of state and head of government

legislature.name: National Assembly (De Nationale Assemblée)
legislature.control: Six-party coalition led by the NDP (34 of 51 seats, a two-thirds majority); the Progressive Reform Party (VHP) is the only opposition party
legislature.detail: 51 seats after the 25 May 2025 election: NDP 18, VHP 17, ABOP 6, NPS 6, PL 2, BEP 1, A20 1. Chairman: Ashwin Adhin (NDP); vice-chairman: Ronnie Brunswijk (ABOP), both since 28 June 2025.

judiciary: The High Court of Justice (Hof van Justitie) heads the ordinary courts, and a Constitutional Court set up in 2019 reviews laws against the constitution. The terms of the Constitutional Court's chair and several members expired on 7 May 2025 without successors being appointed, which has left the court unable to work fully.

elections.name: General election (National Assembly)
elections.note: No party won a majority. The NDP won 18 seats and the governing VHP 17. The NDP then formed a coalition with ABOP, NPS, PL, BEP and A20, which together hold 34 seats. On 6 July 2025 the Assembly elected Jennifer Geerlings-Simons unopposed as the country's first woman president, with Gregory Rusland (NPS) as vice-president. This was the first election under the 2023 electoral reform, which uses proportional representation in a single national constituency.

elections.name: General election (National Assembly)
elections.note: Due by law in 2030, five years after the 2025 election; the Assembly then elects the president and vice-president.

synopsis: Suriname is a republic whose 51-member National Assembly elects the president, who leads both the state and the government. Jennifer Geerlings-Simons of the NDP has been president since 16 July 2025 and leads a six-party coalition that holds exactly the two-thirds majority needed to elect a president. The VHP of former president Chan Santokhi, who died in March 2026, is the only opposition party. The government's main focus is preparing for expected offshore oil and gas revenue.
policies: Preparing the state for offshore oil and gas production and planning how to use the revenue for long-term savings, national development, healthcare and housing
Digitising government services, presented as a way to reduce corruption
Setting up a presidential working group on land rights and decentralisation affecting Indigenous and Maroon communities
Reforming tax collection and tightening regulation of the gold sector and its money flows
Seeking investment through diplomacy and expanding regional and international partnerships
challenges: Keeping together a six-party coalition whose two-thirds margin is thin, after strains such as the October 2026 dispute over the head of the telecoms regulator
A Constitutional Court that cannot work fully because most of its members are serving on expired terms
Power-generation shortfalls and financial pressure on state companies such as Surinam Airways
Managing public finances and expectations ahead of oil income
Crime, public security and informal gold mining in the interior
reviewNote: Not confirmed: reports that President Simons called in November 2026 for the Constitutional Court to be re-staffed and for its law to be changed so that its rulings can be appealed.

name: Uruguay
system: Unitary presidential republic with a bicameral General Assembly

legislature.name: Chamber of Senators
legislature.control: Frente Amplio (majority)
legislature.detail: 30 elected seats (2024): Frente Amplio 16, National Party 9, Colorado Party 5. Vice President Carolina Cosse (Frente Amplio) presides.

legislature.name: Chamber of Representatives
legislature.control: No majority: Frente Amplio is the largest party, and the opposition together holds a majority
legislature.detail: 99 seats (2024): Frente Amplio 48, National Party 29, Colorado Party 17, Identidad Soberana 2, Cabildo Abierto 2, Independent Party 1

judiciary: The Supreme Court of Justice is the highest court and also rules on whether laws are constitutional. Its five members are elected by a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly, so the government and the opposition have to agree on them, as they did when Álvaro França was appointed in 2026.

elections.name: General election (presidential run-off)
elections.note: Yamandú Orsi (Frente Amplio) beat Álvaro Delgado (National Party) with 52.08% to 47.92%. In the 27 October 2024 first round, Frente Amplio won a Senate majority (16 of 30) and 48 of 99 seats in the Chamber of Representatives.

elections.name: General election (president and General Assembly)
elections.note: Due by law in October 2029, with a presidential run-off in November if needed

synopsis: Uruguay is a presidential republic in which the president is both head of state and head of government. Yamandú Orsi of the centre-left Frente Amplio took office on 1 March 2025 after winning the November 2024 run-off. His coalition holds a Senate majority but needs opposition votes in the Chamber of Representatives.
policies: Encouraging large foreign investment, including a preliminary agreement signed in October 2026 with Spain's Solaria for data centres and solar power, which the government calls the largest investment in the country's history
Raising contributions to the reformed professionals' pension fund (CJPPU), set by decree in November 2025 (20.5% in 2026, rising to 22.5% in 2028)
Negotiating the purchase of new offshore patrol vessels, with France's Naval Group among the bidders, after cancelling the previous government's contract with the Spanish shipyard Cardama
Coordinating policy through regular Councils of Ministers with the governing Frente Amplio
challenges: Low public approval of the government: 19% approve and 52% disapprove in a November 2026 Opción poll
No majority in the Chamber of Representatives, so laws need opposition support
Financing defence purchases and other spending while keeping public finances under control

name: Venezuela
system: Federal presidential republic under an acting president, in a transition overseen by the United States after Nicolás Maduro was captured by US forces in January 2026

legislature.name: National Assembly (Asamblea Nacional)
legislature.control: PSUV-led Great Patriotic Pole Simón Bolívar (GPPSB) majority; president Jorge Rodríguez (PSUV), re-elected to the post on 5 January 2026
legislature.detail: Unicameral, 285 seats; elected 25 May 2025, when the main opposition faction led by María Corina Machado boycotted the vote. The current term began on 5 January 2026.

judiciary: The Supreme Tribunal of Justice (TSJ, 32 seats) is the top court. It has long been seen as aligned with the chavista government, and a rival TSJ appointed by the opposition-led legislature in 2017 sits in exile. Under an August 2026 agreement between the government and part of the opposition, the National Assembly reformed the TSJ law, gave civil society a majority on the judicial nominations committee and began replacing all the justices; nominations close on 18 November 2026, and the US Secretary of State has said the new justices should be in place by mid-December.

elections.name: National Assembly and regional elections
elections.note: The PSUV-led Great Patriotic Pole won a large majority. The main opposition faction led by María Corina Machado boycotted the vote. This is the most recent national vote; the July 2024 presidential result, which declared Maduro the winner, was disputed by the opposition and many foreign governments.

elections.name: Presidential election
elections.note: Not yet scheduled. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said elections should ideally be held in 2027, after the Supreme Court and the National Electoral Council have been renewed. María Corina Machado is calling for elections in 2027.

elections.name: National Assembly election
elections.note: Due by law at the end of the five-year term that began in January 2026; no date has been set.

synopsis: Delcy Rodríguez, Nicolás Maduro's vice president, has been acting president since 5 January 2026, two days after US forces captured Maduro, and she continued past the 90-day limit the Supreme Tribunal set for her role. Her PSUV government is following a phased transition plan backed by the United States: an amnesty law, renewal of the Supreme Court and the electoral council, and then elections, for which no date has been set. Opposition leader María Corina Machado returned from exile in October 2026.
policies: Opening the oil sector to US companies, including a non-binding memorandum of understanding signed with Exxon Mobil in November 2026 to assess oil projects
Amnesty Law for Democratic Coexistence (February 2026) and the release of political prisoners
Replacing all Supreme Court justices and creating a new National Electoral Council under an August 2026 agreement between the government and part of the opposition
Diplomatic and security cooperation with the United States, including the appointment of Oliver Blanco as foreign minister in October 2026
challenges: No date set for a presidential election, and disputes over the pace and legitimacy of the transition
Economic hardship and public-sector pay disputes, including a teachers' and health workers' strike called for 16 November 2026
Accountability for human rights abuses documented by the UN Fact-Finding Mission
Rebuilding judicial and electoral independence after decades of political control
Armed groups such as the ELN, and recovery from the June 2026 earthquakes
reviewNote: In flux: Delcy Rodríguez is serving as acting president after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in January 2026; a US-backed transition is under way, with the Supreme Court and electoral council being renewed and no election date set. Not confirmed: the seat counts from the 25 May 2025 National Assembly election; whether Rodríguez still holds the Vice Presidency or has named a new executive vice president; and whether she has formally become PSUV president.
